title: Chapter 156: Who Is Following Me?
html:
“Who’s there?” Mallet raised, Chen Ge charged down the corridor without hesitation, determined to give the intruder no time to react.

“Come out!”

With the entrance locked, whoever was inside already knew he had arrived. He had nothing left to conceal.

Man and cat raced around the stairwell corner, but only darkness waited above them. Whatever had been there was gone.

“Where did it go?” He had tested the white cat repeatedly at the Haunted House. Its sensitivity to unnatural things had never failed him.

The cat showed aggression without flying into a frenzy, so this presence should be less dangerous than whatever inhabits Mu Yang High School.

The white cat had reacted violently only twice before: inside the Mu Yang High School scenario and when the blood door appeared in the bathroom. Comparing those responses gave Chen Ge a rough measure of the current threat.

The real problem is that I don’t know whether it was human or a ghost.

Back at the nurses’ station, he smashed apart the counter and pried away its wooden panel. What lay beneath was deeply unsettling. Bundles of hair, each bound with string, had been nailed to the board. “Why would anyone nail hair here? What does it mean?”

Each bundle had been tied with care. One was soft, dark, and lustrous, probably from a young woman who maintained it meticulously. Another was coarse and white with split ends, likely from an elderly person. Comparing color, texture, and length, Chen Ge determined that the samples came from four individuals.

“At least one of these four people must still be alive.” He studied the two iron cages, their purpose slowly becoming clear. “I’m dealing with people who are genuinely dangerous.”

Setting the panel aside, he crouched again. This time, he could read the tiny message on the wall: I will repay everything you have done to me.

More senseless lines surrounded it. The writer seemed to have been interrupted midway through a coherent thought and fallen into rambling.

“Some patients mutter incoherently during an episode, much as ordinary people talk in their sleep.” Chen Ge tried to decipher the words, but they resisted interpretation.

A chill crept up his spine as he read. The writing resembled the sentences covering the hospital’s outer walls: each mentioned a name, and the varying handwriting suggested many authors. A few patients sharing the behavior would have been understandable—but an entire hospital?

“It seems every patient here had unfinished business.” Chen Ge photographed the writing beneath the nurses’ station, then tied the rooster to his backpack. “Still, the more people involved, the more likely someone is to make a mistake. Time to enter the second sick hall.”

Chen Ge climbed out of the station and opened a packet of salt. He sprinkled a thin line around the counter—not to ward off evil, but to expose the hidden intruder’s footprints. Carrying the open packet, he approached the passage connecting the first and second sick halls. Just before he crossed over, the white cat leaped onto a windowsill and clawed at the glass.

“Careful. You’ll fall.” Chen Ge joined it at the window. Dense woods surrounded the hospital, and no light was visible anywhere.

“Who would imagine a building this large hidden in the middle of nowhere?” He saw nothing unusual, yet the cat refused to leave, raising its head and meowing insistently.

“Is something wrong with the window? Or is it above us?” He opened the window and looked up. Directly overhead, a twisted face stared down from the third floor. Backlit and shadowed, the figure recoiled at the sound of the opening window and disappeared without bothering to close its own.

“That face…” Chen Ge had not expected his adversary to appear so suddenly. Their eyes met for less than a tenth of a second, too briefly for a clear view. He knew only that the face looked wrong, though he could not identify why.

He went still and listened. No footsteps sounded, suggesting the figure had not fled down the corridor. “The two sides of the face seemed uneven, but I think it was human.”

He entered the second sick hall expecting a copy of the first, only to find a completely different layout. This building was larger and more spacious, with no beds crowding its corridors. Chairs, tables, and lamps stood between the rooms.

“The conditions here were clearly better.” Chen Ge scattered a handful of salt near the stairs, then entered the closest room. Someone had ripped open the mattress and strewn its stuffing everywhere. A chamber pot sat beside the eating utensils, and fingernails had gouged countless characters into the wall.

“Caring for these patients every day could not have been easy.” He left the room and continued onward.

The second sick hall contained a wider variety of rooms: specialized isolation cells, recreation and chess rooms, showers, and even a small auditorium at the corridor’s end. Its decoration, however, was deeply peculiar.

The auditorium had not been prepared for a party or dance. Heavy curtains covered sealed windows, and every decoration was black or white. Before Chen Ge even crossed the threshold, he spotted an enormous black-and-white portrait at the center of the stage.

The portrait hung on the wall, slashed in half by an unknown hand. The surviving section showed a broad, middle-aged nurse with a scowl on her face.

“An enlarged black-and-white portrait, heavy curtains, rows of wooden chairs… Why does this look like a funeral hall?” He could not understand why the hospital would host such a ceremony—or what it had been intended to mean.

“Was this nurse a victim of the Third Sick Hall? If so, why display her portrait here in the second?”

After memorizing the nurse’s face, Chen Ge closed the door, laid a line of salt across the threshold, and hurried upstairs to the third floor.
